label: prop:operator-selection-lp
title: Knot operator selection as linear program with LP duality
html:
Let n \geq 2, let \{b_1, \ldots, b_d\} be a basis of H_n(q) (the NF basis, with d = n!), let t_i = \mathrm{tr}_M(b_i) be the Markov traces, let G_{ij} = \mathrm{tr}_M(b_i \cdot b_j) be the d \times d Frobenius Gram matrix, and let n_{\mathrm{target}} \in \mathbb{R}_{>0} be a target net value. Consider the linear program

  \min_{x \in \mathbb{R}^d} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{d} t_i \, x_i

subject to:

  \sum_{i=1}^{d} x_i = n_{\mathrm{target}}
  \qquad (\text{net constraint})
  \sum_{j=1}^{d} G_{ij}\, x_j \geq 0
  \quad \forall\, i \in \{1, \ldots, d\}
  \qquad (\text{Frobenius positivity})
  x_i \geq -M \quad \forall\, i
  \qquad (\text{boundedness})

where M > 0 is a constant large enough to ensure boundedness of the feasible polyhedron. Any minimiser \Phi^* = \sum_{i} x_i^* b_i lies in H_n(q) and satisfies every Frobenius positivity and net constraint; the dual certificate (y_0^*, y^*) certifies optimality.

Degeneracy of this program

Two properties of the program as stated, both proved and neither previously recorded. They are stated here because downstream blocks have read the program as a selection principle, which it is not.

The optimal value is identically zero. The NF basis begins with the empty word, so b_1 = \mathbf{1} and hence

G_{1j} \;=\; \mathrm{tr}_M(\mathbf{1}\cdot b_j) \;=\; t_j .

The first row of the Gram matrix is the objective vector, so the Frobenius positivity constraint at i = 1 reads \sum_j t_j x_j \geq 0 — the objective itself, bounded below by zero. The program therefore minimises t\cdot x subject to t\cdot x \geq 0, and its optimal value is 0 whenever it is feasible. This requires only that the basis contain the identity, so it holds for every n, every q, and every trace convention. By strong duality n_{\mathrm{target}}\cdot y_0^* = 0 with n_{\mathrm{target}} > 0, so y_0^* = 0: the net constraint carries no shadow price, and n_{\mathrm{target}} cannot influence the objective.

The set of minimisers is not a point. It is \{x : \sum_i x_i = n_{\mathrm{target}},\; (Gx)_1 = 0,\; (Gx)_i \geq 0\ (i \geq 2)\}, a positive-dimensional face. At n = 3 it carries at least six vertices, all at objective 0, occurring in mirror pairs under \sigma_0 \leftrightarrow \sigma_1. Since t and G are mirror-invariant the optimal set is mirror-closed, so a unique minimiser would have to be mirror-symmetric; none of these vertices is. The program therefore does not determine a distinguished \Phi^*, and which vertex a solver returns is a property of its pivoting rule.

Dual program (demand pricing)

The primal variable x is free apart from the box x_i \ge -M, so the dual constraints are equalities. With multipliers y_0 (free) for the net constraint, y_i \ge 0 for the Frobenius constraints and w_i \ge 0 for the box, the dual is:

  \max_{y_0,\, y,\, w} \quad n_{\mathrm{target}} \cdot y_0 - M \sum_{i=1}^{d} w_i

subject to:

  y_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{d} G_{ij}\, y_i + w_j \;=\; t_j
  \quad \forall\, j \in \{1, \ldots, d\}
  y_i \geq 0, \quad w_i \geq 0 \quad \forall\, i

If no box constraint is active at the optimum, then w^* = 0 and the dual reduces to:

  \max_{y_0, \, y \geq 0} \quad n_{\mathrm{target}} \cdot y_0

subject to:

  y_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{d} G_{ij}\, y_i \;=\; t_j
  \quad \forall\, j \in \{1, \ldots, d\}

The inequality form y_0 + \sum_i G_{ij} y_i \le t_j is the dual of the program with x \ge 0, not of this one. Because G_{1j} = t_j for b_1 = 1, the point y_0 = 0, y = e_1, w = 0 is dual-feasible with value 0, which matches the primal optimum above.

Strong duality

Proposition (strong duality). The primal and dual programs have equal optimal values:

  \sum_{i=1}^{d} t_i \, x_i^*
  \;=\;
  n_{\mathrm{target}} \cdot y_0^* - M \sum_{i=1}^{d} w_i^*,

which equals n_{\mathrm{target}} \cdot y_0^* when no box constraint is active.
